plainLanguageExplanation: Andromeda, also cataloged M31, is the nearest big galaxy outside the Milky Way. It is about 2.5 million light-years away — a distance so comfortable that its light left around the time the first tools were being made in Africa. Despite that distance, it is the farthest thing you can see with the naked eye on a dark night: it looks like a faint oval patch in the constellation Andromeda (the galaxy's name comes from the mythic princess), and with binoculars it turns into a glowing spindle. It is a classic, smooth spiral — no central bar — with about a trillion stars, up to twice the Milky Way's star count, and a bright bulge and a nucleus hosting a supermassive black hole of over 100 million solar masses. And it is coming toward us. The two galaxies — whole galaxies, a hundred thousand light-years across — are falling together at about 110 kilometers per second, and in roughly four billion years they will merge into a single, larger, mostly elliptical galaxy (nicknamed 'Milkomeda'). But this is a merge of two crowds, almost no star collision: the interleaving space there is so gloriously empty that the stars will pass without touching.

whyItMatters: Andromeda is the Milky Way's nearest reference object: it shows what our galaxy looks like from outside, because someone could photograph it far better than we can photograph ourselves. Its being visible without a telescope is also the finest live proof that the universe is full of galaxies — what looks like a smudge in the sky is really a trillion suns, and tens of thousands of similar smudges own the deep sky. And the known meeting in four billion years is astronomy's best current 'future,' making the sky feel real, moving, and interactive rather than static — a model of what galactic life actually is.
scientificName: Messier 31 (M31), Sb-type spiral, nearest large galaxy
tagline: The galaxy that's coming our way
didYouKnow: Andromeda's light takes 2.5 million years to reach you — so when you look at it, you are seeing the galaxy as it was before the first humans became a word, and what you see as a pale smudge holds more stars than every grain of sand on Earth.
